TITLE: What six grazing horses tell us about England's housing crisis - BBC News

IrelandScotlandAlbaWalesCymruIsle of ManGuernseyJerseyLocal NewsWhat six grazing horses tell us about England's housing crisisTo play this video you need to enable JavaScript in your browser.This video can not be played

Watch: What happened to the 7,400 homes promised across these three developments?

About a five-minute walk from the train station in Middlesbrough, six horses are grazing lazily on a derelict patch of land.

Tethered and friendly, the animals do not attract much attention from residents, despite being so close to the town centre.

But their presence on the land, by the banks of the River Tees, is a symbol of the UK's decades-long failure to build enough houses.

In 2004, the local council announced plans to build 2,400 homes on the grass the horses are eating.

But 22 years later, just 216 homes have been built. The money initially outlined for the project has never been found.

The UK is in a housing crisis with demand for homes continuing to outstrip supply.

To understand why successive governments have failed to build enough houses, BBC News went to this Middlesbrough scheme, and planned developments in York and the Isle of Sheppey, in Kent.

Each has its own story, with finances, infrastructure planning and developers' appetites all playing a major role - issues mirrored at other sites across the country.

Combined, the projects we visited promised to build 7,400 homes. To date, just 326 have been constructed.

Shortfalls like this affect national goals significantly, says Anthony Breach, director of policy and research at the Centre for Cities think tank.

The UK's reliance on "large, complex schemes" to deliver new housing means that "when our larger sites get a bit stuck, that has a disproportionate impact on national housebuilding", he says.

These large-scale projects, increasingly favoured by private developers and often driven by local councils, are key to the Labour government's target of building 1.5 million homes in England by the next election.

That target will probably be missed.

The 2004 plans for Middlehaven in Middlesbrough, a long-disused industrial site, included not just thousands of homes but also a theatre, restaurants and hotels.

It was billed as a £500m development, but it had one fundamental flaw: the money never existed.

Instead, this figure was simply an estimate of overall cost, Middlesbrough Council told us.

Almost a decade later, in 2013, the development was proposed again. This time, the council bought 185 homes that already existed, so they could be demolished to make space.

Yet only 216 homes have been built to replace them, a net gain of 31.

Image caption, Some buildings, like these offices, have been constructed on the Middlesbrough site

The council says delivery of the masterplan was curtailed by the 2008 financial crash, "leading to the departure of the council's development partner".

A college campus, business space and housing have been delivered, it says, and a new school is being built.

The price that new homes will sell for is a key factor in large developments progressing, says Breach, as housebuilding firms look for returns on their investments.

In places where house prices are lower, he says, public sector funds may be needed to "bridge the gap between the cost of building [works] and the price at which the houses can be sold for".

In September, Middlesbrough Council announced plans for 462 new homes on the site - the beginning, it hopes, of a development of 3,400 homes in all.

This time, however, the council is far more cautious, acknowledging the money might not be there to achieve everything it would like.

In York, a plan for 3,000 homes was announced in 2001, but a quarter of a century later, not a single house has been built.

Alongside the homes, close to the historic centre of the city, were to be business and hospitality opportunities - just like in Middlesbrough.

Image caption, The site in York that is yet to be developed

Planning consultant Nora Galley was hired by the local council to develop the York Central masterplan.

Her designs, she tells the BBC, combined a realistic vision with a plan to deliver it.

"It wasn't just a beautiful place that looked great in architect's drawings," she says.

But by the time the 2008 crash hit, work had not begun.

In September this year, the project's first phase was finally given the green light, with some 2,500 homes planned to be built by 2040.

Image caption, "There is no fabric in this country to manage the delivery of strategic projects," says Nora Galley

Galley is disappointed that construction has taken so long to get under way, and that fewer homes will be built than originally planned.

"There is no fabric in this country to manage the delivery of strategic projects," she tells us - highlighting what she sees as supply chain issues and a lack of construction training.

In June, trade body the Construction Industry Training Board, external backed Galley's point - citing a need for 206,000 new construction workers across the UK between now and 2030.

York Central is now set to cost £2bn to complete, far more than the hundreds of millions of pounds local papers reported when plans were first set out.

Delays to the project have cost York greatly, says Galley. The city has missed out on "wealth, opportunities, a better-performing economy".

Image caption, The first houses should be built within two years, says Claire Douglas, leader of City of York Council

Residents we spoke to were largely in favour of York Central, seeing its potential. But all seemed puzzled by the amount of time it had taken.

Cycle lanes, pristine paths and bus stops surround the site, yet nobody was around to use them. "I had colour in my hair when they first announced it," quips one middle-aged woman who lives in the neighbouring estate.

The main problem has been the site's positioning, surrounded by railway lines, says Labour leader of City of York Council, Claire Douglas.

The project stalled because, for a time, there was no money from government to pay for an access road allowing construction materials on to the site, she says.

But now the access road is nearing completion and the first houses should be built within two years, she says.

Nearly 200 miles (322km) south, on the Isle of Sheppey in Kent, a planned development of up to 2,000 new homes was meant to help regenerate a deprived part of the island.

It is now 23 years since the plan was initially conceived, and 17 years since it was backed by local councils. But only 110 houses have been built.

The project was hailed in a 2009 press release as a "£400m regeneration" of the area, but Swale Borough Council has told the BBC that, as in Middlesbrough, the money never actually existed.

The figure, it said, was an estimation "of the likely investment required to deliver the scheme at that time", and there was no housing developer lined up.

Image caption, A development of 2,000 homes was planned to be built at this site on the Isle of Sheppey

Some 3,000 jobs were also expected to be created, but only some have materialised.

A retail park housing a Morrisons, Burger King and Sports Direct among other outlets has been completed, but plans for a marina have been scrapped.

Where the hundreds of homes should stand is an empty field surrounded by metal railings. Locals say the grass is occasionally mowed.

Meanwhile, the council has 1,800 households waiting for social housing.

"We do need a few more houses [here], but we also need more doctors and things like that as well," says Marie Miller, lifelong resident of the neighbouring village of Rushenden.

Image caption, Along with new homes, local amenities need to be provided, says resident Marie Miller

The planned "state of the art" healthcare centre on the same site remains unbuilt.

Nothing has happened on the site in a long time, Miller says.

The original 2,000-homes plan was scaled back in 2015 to 1,180, but even this reduced figure is unlikely to be achieved. According to council documents, the project is back at the planning stage.

Homes England, the government's housing and regeneration agency, is now approaching housebuilders for their "early observations" about developing the site.

After the economic downturn of 2008, the planned level of development "proved to be an optimistic forecast", the local council said, adding it was "working closely with Homes England to agree an updated timescale".

These three schemes we have visited are not the only projects to have failed to deliver new housing over long time periods.

In London, where housebuilding has fallen substantially in recent years, not one of the 3,500 homes planned for Convoy's Wharf in Deptford has been built - despite outline planning permission being given in 2005. Planning problems and objections from locals have contributed to the delays.

On the north side of the Thames, a 2008 plan to build 10,800 units at Barking Riverside was stalled for years because of poor transport links. However, since the creation of a new rail line, 3,000 homes now have been built and plans have been approved to almost double the housing development to 20,000 homes.

The glacial speed at which things get done, particularly at the sites we visited in Middlesbrough, York and Kent, offer key insights as to why the UK has not built as many homes as it needs.

Image caption, Local politicians may deny planning applications even if developers follow all the rules, says Anthony Breach

Part of the housebuilding challenge, says Anthony Breach from Centre for Cities, is that the UK's planning system is "pretty unusual internationally".

Even if a developer follows all the rules "you can still be denied planning permission by local politicians", he says - meaning developments take much longer, and risk being upended if a new party is elected locally.

To overcome planning delays, mayoral development corporations (MDCs) are increasingly being established by England's regional mayors. These bodies can take planning duties away from a local authority and make compulsory land purchases, enabling large-scale projects to move more quickly.

Breach sees this as a positive step, describing MDCs as a shortcut through the planning system that should see housebuilding increase.

A spokesperson for the Ministry of Housing told the BBC it was "working with Homes England to get stalled schemes moving, with housing starts up 20% on this time last year".

They added: "We've unblocked and accelerated more than 130,000 homes and, through our planning overhaul and £40bn Social and Affordable Homes Programme, we are unlocking development and building the homes our country needs."

The schemes in Middlesbrough, York and Kent may eventually come good - but decades later than promised, their failures all contributing to the UK's chronic lack of housing.
